focus: Runtime decoders vs declared TypeScript types. For each decoder: does it actually validate, or does it cast and trust the server? Check optional vs required drift, null vs undefined, number parsing of decimal strings, enum member sets that must match the backend exactly (a value the decoder rejects blanks that field in the UI; a value it accepts but the UI cannot render is equally bad), date parsing, array element validation, and whether a decoder throws or silently returns a partial object on bad input. A decoder that rejects a legitimate server value is a P1 because it breaks a real page.

safeUrl: origin canonicalisation and path joining. Can a caller-supplied id or query value escape the intended path (../ traversal, protocol-relative //evil.com, absolute URL override, encoded slashes, userinfo @ tricks)? Is the allowed origin checked by prefix (bypassable by evil-origin.com) or by parsed origin equality? problemDetails: RFC7807 parsing of untrusted responses, missing-field handling, and whether raw server detail text is surfaced to the UI in a way that could inject markup or leak internals.

The route table and navigation model. Check: every declared route reachable and every nav target declared; unknown/unmatched route behaviour (blank screen vs 404); deep-link handling on first load before auth resolves; order of auth guard vs route render (does a protected page flash its content before redirect); route params parsed and validated; back/forward and history state; and any route that renders a destructive action reachable without confirmation.

Shell correctness: active-route highlighting logic (prefix matching that marks the wrong item active), nav state after route change, keyboard navigation and focus order, ARIA landmarks and labels, mobile/collapsed behaviour, and any state held in the shell that goes stale when the underlying data changes.

The shared fetching primitive, so a bug here affects every page. Check: stale closures capturing an old query; a response from a superseded request overwriting a newer one (classic race - is there a request-id or abort guard); cleanup on unmount setting state after teardown; effect dependency arrays causing refetch storms or never refetching; error state not cleared on retry; loading state stuck on when a request is aborted; and whether context value identity changes every render and re-renders the whole tree.

Environment/config parsing. What happens when a required value is missing - does it throw, or silently fall back to a development default that would point production at the wrong API or disable a security check? Check any dev-only flag that could be enabled in a production build, values baked into the bundle at build time that should not be public, and boolean parsing of string env vars (the classic Boolean('false') === true bug).

Token handling in the browser. Where is the token stored (localStorage is readable by any injected script; in-memory or httpOnly cookie is safer) and is it cleared on logout and on tab close? Check PKCE presence and correctness, state/nonce validation against CSRF and replay, redirect_uri validation, token expiry and refresh, and whether the token is ever put in a URL or logged. Critically: developmentOidc is a development identity path - determine exactly what gates it and whether a production build can reach it. A dev auth bypass shipped to production is a P0.

This is the page a trader reads first, so a wrong number here is a real defect. Check derived values and aggregates computed client-side, number and currency formatting (locale, decimal places, rounding, negative sign placement), percentage math, division by zero producing NaN or Infinity rendered to screen, empty/loading/error states, and stale data shown without any indication it is stale.

List and detail state, polling of a running backtest (interval cleanup on unmount, backoff, stop condition when the run completes or fails), equity curve rendering (downsampling that misrepresents drawdown, axis scaling, missing points), result metric formatting, and the create flow - double-submit prevention, validation errors surfaced, and what happens if the request succeeds but the response fails to decode.

Pure validation logic, so it is fully testable and worth checking exactly. Date range validation (start after end, future dates, timezone of the parsed date shifting the range by a day), numeric coercion of deposit and leverage (empty string to 0, NaN, negative, exponent notation), required-field checks, and any validation that is enforced in the UI but not on the server (or vice versa - a field the server rejects that the form allows).

This edits LIVE TRADING parameters, so it is the highest-risk frontend surface. Check lot size and risk-percentage input handling (coercion, bounds, decimal precision, whether an empty or malformed value becomes 0 or NaN and is then sent), start/stop actions and whether they are confirmed and protected against double-click, optimistic UI that shows a bot as running when the request failed, whether settings are sent as a full replacement (silently resetting fields the form did not load) or a patch, and stale-write risk when two tabs edit the same bot.

Polling and lifecycle. Check every setInterval/setTimeout for clearing on unmount and on dependency change, polling that continues after the component is gone (leak) or after a terminal state is reached, unbounded retry without backoff hammering the API, state set after unmount, and race between a probe result and a newer user action. Also check whether the development probe hook can run in a production build.

Broker credentials pass through this code in the browser. Check whether a password or investor password is ever placed in component state longer than needed, logged, put in a URL or query string, included in an error message, or retained after submission. Check validation of login/server/password fields, and whether the model distinguishes an investor (read-only) password from a trading password - conflating them is a real risk.

Catalog list state (paging, sort stability, filter reset), detail fetch and error handling, and above all: strategy SOURCE CODE and vendor-supplied metadata (name, description, author) are UNTRUSTED input rendered in the UI. Check for dangerouslySetInnerHTML, any HTML injection path, and unescaped rendering of source or metadata. Also check very large source files rendered without virtualisation freezing the page.

Compile status polling and log rendering. Compiler output is derived from untrusted user source, so check how logs and diagnostics are rendered (any dangerouslySetInnerHTML or unescaped HTML is an XSS path), unbounded log growth freezing the browser, polling cleanup and stop conditions, and whether a failed compile is clearly distinguished from a successful one in the UI state machine.

Journal: paging and filter correctness, timestamp timezone rendering, P&L formatting and sign. Cloud: runner/plan state and any provisioning action. Settings: destructive or account-level actions - are they confirmed, are they idempotent against double-click, and is a failure surfaced rather than silently swallowed leaving the UI showing the new state.

LaunchWizard puts a strategy into live trading, so its state machine is safety-critical: can a step be skipped, can the final submit fire twice, is the accumulated state validated before submit, and is a partially completed launch left in a bad state on error? For all three: focus trap and restore on close, Escape handling, backdrop click discarding unsaved input, and submit-in-flight disabling.

scope: src/Frontend/YO4X.Web/src/shared/ui/*.tsx (Badge, BrandMark, Chip, Drawer, EmptyState, Icon, Modal, Panel, Skeleton, Stars, StatTile, Thumb, Toggle)
focus: Reused primitives, so a defect multiplies. Modal/Drawer: focus trap, focus restore, Escape, aria-modal and role, background scroll lock, portal cleanup. Toggle: is it a real checkbox/switch with keyboard support and aria-checked, or a div that only responds to click? Icon: any SVG built from an untrusted string. StatTile: number formatting and overflow. General: missing accessible names, and click handlers on non-interactive elements.

scope:
src/Frontend/YO4X.Web/src/app/styles/global.css
src/Frontend/YO4X.Web/src/app/styles/tokens.css
all feature CSS: auth/auth.css, features/backtests/backtests.css, features/bots/bots.css, features/cloud/cloud.css, features/compiler/compiler.css, features/dashboard/dashboard.css, features/journal/journal.css, features/overlays/overlays.css, features/settings/settings.css, features/strategies/catalog.css, features/strategies/detail.css
focus: Design-token discipline: hardcoded colours that bypass tokens, tokens defined only inside a media query or theme block so one theme has no value, and colour pairs that fail WCAG AA contrast (especially profit-green/loss-red on the dark surface, and any status colour that is the ONLY signal distinguishing profit from loss - colour-blind users then cannot read the P&L). Also: fixed pixel heights that clip content, z-index conflicts between modal/drawer/toast, and horizontal overflow on narrow viewports.

Build and delivery security. Check: is a Content-Security-Policy defined anywhere, and does index.html allow inline script; are source maps emitted in the production build (shipping readable source and comments); dev proxy settings that leak into production; any env var exposed to the client bundle that should not be (anything not intentionally public); dependency versions with known CVEs and whether they are pinned or floating (^ ranges); and integrity of any external script or font loaded from a CDN.

scope:
src/Frontend/YO4X.Web/src/**/*.test.ts and *.test.tsx (contracts.test.ts, controlPlaneClient.test.ts, safeUrl.test.ts, runtimeConfig.test.ts, AuthEntry.test.tsx, developmentOidc.test.ts, backtestForm.test.ts, backtests.test.tsx, BotSettingsModal.test.tsx, BotsPage.test.tsx, brokerRegistration.test.ts, LinkAccountModal.test.tsx)
src/Frontend/YO4X.Web/src/tests/setup.ts
focus: Do these tests actually constrain behaviour? Look for: assertions that only check a render did not throw; mocks so complete that the real code path is never exercised; snapshot tests that would happily absorb a regression; tests asserting on implementation detail rather than behaviour; and the specific untested branches that matter (error paths, validation rejection, race handling). Name the concrete branch and the bug it would hide - do not file a generic 'needs more tests'.

scope: src/Frontend/YO4X.Web/scripts/design-capture.mjs, dom-probe.mjs, interaction-check.mjs, live-capture.mjs, live-detail.mjs, stub-api.mjs, visual-qa.mjs
focus: These scripts produce the QA evidence the team trusts. The key question: does stub-api.mjs still match the real API contract, or has it drifted so QA passes against a fiction? Compare its shapes to src/api/contracts.ts. Also check whether the capture/probe scripts assert anything or merely take screenshots, whether a failure exits non-zero, and any hardcoded credential or URL.

Every endpoint: is authorisation applied, and is the caller's ownership of the id in the route actually verified before returning or mutating (an IDOR here exposes another tenant's trading data)? Also check model binding and validation of the request body, status codes (a 200 returned on a failed operation), error responses leaking internal detail or stack traces, route parameter parsing and bounds (limit/paging values that are unbounded or negative), and whether mutation endpoints require an idempotency key.

Host composition. Middleware ORDER (authentication before authorisation before endpoints; exception handling outermost; anything mapped before auth is unauthenticated). CORS policy - any AllowAnyOrigin combined with credentials is a serious defect. DI lifetimes: a scoped service (DbConnection, tenant context) captured by a singleton is a classic cross-request data leak - check every registration. Also HTTPS enforcement, security headers, whether developer exception pages or Swagger are conditional on environment, and what the readiness probe actually proves.

Credential handling and claim trust. In the vault: where credentials are stored, whether they are encrypted at rest, whether plaintext lingers in memory/logs/exceptions, and access control on retrieval. In WorkloadActorClaims: is the actor identity derived from a validated token, or from a header/claim the caller can set themselves (that would be an authentication bypass, P0)? In the development probe: exactly what prevents it running in production, and does it handle real credentials.

BFF pattern security: token relay (does it forward the user token, exchange it, or use a privileged service credential - the last would let any authenticated user act with admin rights downstream), which downstream endpoints it exposes and whether it narrows or widens the surface, CORS and cookie settings (SameSite, Secure, HttpOnly), CSRF protection on state-changing routes, and authorisation on every admin action.

This endpoint receives secret material, so it is a primary attack surface. Check: proof/signature validation before the payload is trusted, and whether the comparison is constant-time (a non-constant-time equality on a MAC is a real timing oracle); replay protection via nonce, timestamp window, or one-time token; rate limiting and payload size limits; where the ingested secret goes and whether it is ever logged or echoed in a response or error; TLS enforcement; and the failure mode - does a validation error fail closed.

This is the kill switch - it must work under the worst conditions and must not be triggerable by the wrong party. Check: authorisation on the trigger endpoint; idempotency (triggering twice must be safe); whether the stop is synchronous and confirmed or fire-and-forget; what happens if a downstream dependency is down (it must still fail SAFE, i.e. stop trading rather than silently no-op); whether there is an un-trigger path and who can call it; and whether the endpoint is reachable and healthy independently of the main control plane.

A development identity provider that issues tokens. The central question: what EXACTLY prevents this from running or being reachable in production, and is that guard robust (a build-time exclusion is strong; a runtime env-var check is weak if the var can be unset or misspelled)? Also: the token signing key - is it hardcoded or a well-known default, and do other services accept tokens signed by it; what claims can a caller request (can a user mint an admin token); token lifetime; and whether the project is referenced by any production host.

Shared API infrastructure, so a defect here applies to every host. Check the exception-handling middleware (does it leak stack traces, inner exception messages, or SQL text to the client in any environment), problem-details construction, validation filters and whether a validation failure can be bypassed, any shared authorisation helper and its default when a policy is absent, correlation/trace id handling, and any middleware that could swallow an exception and return 200.

scope: src/Apps/YO4X.ControlPlane.Workers/Operations/ - all files EXCEPT PostgresUserOperationWorkStore.cs (ControlWorkBackgroundService.cs, ControlWorkContracts.cs, ControlWorkOptions.cs, ControlWorkReadiness.cs, PostgresCredentialGrantExpiryStore.cs, PostgresDeploymentProjectionStore.cs, PostgresWorkerInfrastructure.cs, PostgresWorkerRegistration.cs, UserOperationDispatchEnvelope.cs, WorkerPolicySignatureTrustStore.cs, WorkerTenantScanCoordinator.cs)
focus: The background service loop: exception handling inside the loop (an unhandled exception that kills the loop silently stops all work), cancellation token propagation and graceful shutdown mid-operation, polling interval and backoff on empty or on error. WorkerTenantScanCoordinator: can it skip a tenant or process one twice, and is the tenant list snapshot consistent. WorkerPolicySignatureTrustStore: signature verification correctness and constant-time comparison, and what happens when verification fails (must fail closed). Credential grant expiry: is expiry enforced on read, not just on write.

Fail-stop semantics: when a fatal condition occurs does the process actually terminate, or log and continue in a degraded state that looks healthy? Check whether the health endpoint can report healthy while the work loop is dead (a liveness probe that only checks the web host is a classic false-green). Check DI lifetimes, graceful shutdown draining in-flight operations, unauthenticated exposure of health endpoints leaking internal state, and the operation boundary's transaction/error handling.

This ingests untrusted third-party MQL5 files, so it is both a state machine and a security boundary. Check: what happens on a malformed, enormous, or maliciously crafted input (unbounded read into memory, zip/decompression bombs, path traversal from a filename inside an archive, symlinks); whether a crash mid-intake leaves an item half-processed and whether re-running is idempotent; whether a poison item blocks the queue forever or is dead-lettered; transaction boundaries between filesystem effects and database state; encoding handling of source files; and resource cleanup of temp files on both success and failure.

scope: src/Apps/YO4X.Conversion.Worker/ - all files EXCEPT Mql5QuarantineIntakeJob.cs (including PostgresMql5CorpusStore.cs ~1043 lines)
focus: Corpus persistence: content hashing and dedup (is the hash over the exact bytes, is a collision or a re-import handled, can the same source land twice under different ids), transaction scope for multi-row writes, large-object/bytea handling and streaming vs loading whole files into memory, tenant scoping, SQL parameterisation, and encoding round-trip fidelity (source stored and read back must be byte-identical or the compile is of different code than was imported).

Desktop host security boundary. If it embeds a WebView: what is the allowed navigation set (can it be navigated to an arbitrary URL), is any host object or IPC bridge exposed to page script and what can it do (filesystem, process launch, credential access), and is the loaded content local or remote. Also check local file and credential access paths, update mechanism if any, and single-instance/protocol-handler argument parsing for injection.

Admin use cases carry the most privilege. Check that each use case verifies the caller is actually an admin rather than assuming the API layer did, that tenant scope is applied on admin reads that should be scoped, input validation on every command, and whether an admin action that affects trading (disabling an account, force-stopping a bot) is audited and idempotent.

Command handling and domain invariants: is every invariant enforced in the handler or only assumed from the UI; are error paths distinguished from success (a handler returning a success result on a caught exception is a P1); transaction boundaries around multi-step operations; validation of user input before it reaches persistence; and idempotency of commands that will be retried.

An evidence/attestation chain is only worth what its weakest link. Check: the hash algorithm (MD5 or SHA1 for integrity is a defect), whether the chain actually links each entry to its predecessor so a middle entry cannot be replaced, whether all security-relevant fields are covered by the hash or only some (an unhashed field can be altered freely), canonical serialisation before hashing (non-deterministic field order or float formatting makes verification flaky or forgeable), any equality comparison on a MAC that is not constant-time, and what happens when verification fails - it must fail closed.

Runtime state transitions for strategies and bots: which transitions are legal, whether an illegal transition is rejected or silently applied, whether a terminal state can be re-entered, concurrent transition handling (two requests both moving a bot from Stopped to Running), and whether the persisted state and the actual runtime state can diverge without detection.

The order lifecycle coordinator - the most money-critical application code. Check: are risk gates evaluated before every order and can any path bypass them; is the command idempotent under retry (a retried submit that places a second order is a P0); ordering guarantees between dependent commands (close before open); what happens when the broker response is unknown or times out (assuming failure and retrying can duplicate an order; assuming success can orphan one); reconciliation of local state against broker state; and error paths that swallow a failure and report success.

Shared primitives, so defects multiply. Check result/either types for a path where an error is constructed but the caller can read a value anyway, guard clauses that do not actually throw, value objects with broken equality or GetHashCode (breaking dictionary lookups silently), any comparison or validation helper with an inverted condition, and any shared static mutable state.

Schema correctness. For each table: is there a tenant column and is it NOT NULL; are foreign keys declared with the right ON DELETE behaviour (a missing FK allows orphans; CASCADE on a financial record silently destroys history); are uniqueness constraints present where the code assumes uniqueness (especially idempotency keys); nullability matching what the code expects; CHECK constraints on enum-like text columns and on non-negative amounts; numeric column types for money (numeric with explicit precision, not double precision or float8); timestamp columns using timestamptz rather than timestamp (a naive timestamp loses the offset and shifts every trade time); and indexes for the predicates the code actually queries on, including the tenant column.

Same schema review as D01 (tenant columns, FKs, uniqueness, CHECKs, money as numeric, timestamptz, indexes). Additionally: 004 provisions development identity - check whether it creates any account, role or credential that would also exist in a production database. For the projection and backtest tables, check numeric precision on result metrics and equity values, and indexes supporting the projection queries.

Same schema review as D01. Specifically: the queue table needs the columns and indexes a FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED claim pattern requires plus a lease/visibility timeout column; the equity curve table needs adequate numeric precision (double precision for equity values is a real precision defect) and an index for time-ordered reads; bot settings need constraints on risk and lot-size columns (non-negative, upper bounds) because these values drive live orders; broker symbols need correct precision for tick size, volume step, min/max volume.

The fail-closed connection policy that recent commits centralised. Verify it actually fails closed: is there any path where a missing or invalid configuration yields a usable connection with default or elevated credentials rather than an exception? Check connection string assembly and whether the password can be logged, SSL/TLS mode (Require vs Prefer - Prefer silently accepts plaintext), pooling settings and whether the tenant/session context is reset when a connection returns to the pool (a leaked SET LOCAL or session variable across pooled connections is a cross-tenant P0), command timeouts, retry policy retrying non-idempotent commands, and transaction isolation defaults.

This asserts the database role has exactly the expected privileges. The critical failure is a FALSE ACCEPT: a fingerprint that matches when the actual grants are broader than expected. Check what is included in the fingerprint and what is omitted (omitted privileges can be silently added), how the expected value is computed and stored, whether comparison is exact or partial, whether ordering/normalisation makes the hash stable, whether a mismatch fails closed (refusing to start) or merely logs, and whether the check runs at startup only or is re-verified.

Write paths. For each mutation: is it inside an explicit transaction covering ALL of its writes (a multi-statement mutation without a transaction can leave half-applied state on failure); is there a concurrency guard (optimistic version, FOR UPDATE) or can a read-then-write lose an update; is the tenant predicate present on every UPDATE and DELETE (a missing tenant clause on an UPDATE can modify another tenant's row - P0); is every value parameterised; is an upsert's conflict target correct; and is a not-found update distinguished from a successful one (checking rows-affected).

scope: src/Infrastructure/YO4X.ControlPlane.Postgres/ControlPlanePostgresOptions.cs, CredentialIngestionProofIssuer.cs, PolicySignatureTrustStore.cs, PostgresBrokerAccountDiscoveryReads.cs, PostgresControlPlaneApplication.cs, PostgresControlPlaneReads.cs, PostgresDeploymentPolicyEvaluation.cs, PostgresDeploymentValidation.cs, PostgresStrategyCompatibilityReads.cs, PostgresUserOperations.cs, ProofKeyRings.cs, StrategyImportProofIssuer.cs
focus: Read authorisation and the proof/key subsystem. On reads: tenant predicate on every query, parameterisation, and unbounded result sets. On the proof issuers and key rings: key rotation correctness (can a token signed by a retired key still validate; is there an overlap window; how is the active key selected), key storage and whether key material can be logged, signature verification using constant-time comparison, and whether a verification failure fails closed. On policy evaluation and deployment validation: can a policy that fails to load be treated as permissive (fail-open) rather than denying.

Runtime state and event persistence: event ordering and whether a sequence/timestamp can collide or go backwards, append-only integrity (can an event be updated or deleted), transaction boundaries between state and events, tenant scoping on every query, parameterisation, and unbounded reads of event history.

Control commands to running strategies. Check locking (advisory locks or row locks) and whether a lock is always released on the error path, whether two controllers can issue conflicting commands concurrently, command ordering and delivery guarantees, tenant scoping, and whether a control command that fails to apply is reported as applied.

Admin data access runs with the highest privilege. Check: does any admin query omit a tenant filter where one is required, or intentionally cross tenants in a way that is not clearly justified and audited; parameterisation of admin search/filter inputs (admin endpoints are often the least sanitised); unbounded queries; and whether write paths are transactional and audited.

Parser fidelity to real MQL5. Check operator PRECEDENCE and ASSOCIATIVITY against the MQL5 table (a single wrong precedence level silently changes what every affected expression computes - e.g. bitwise vs comparison, ternary right-associativity, assignment right-associativity); the dangling-else binding; ternary nesting; cast expression parsing vs parenthesised expression ambiguity; declaration vs expression ambiguity; array declarators and multidimensional arrays; struct/class/enum/input/extern declarations; function pointers and default parameter values; the MQL5 preprocessor interaction; comma operator; and error recovery - does a parse error produce a clear diagnostic or silently skip a construct (silently dropping a statement is a P0 because the compiled strategy then trades differently from its source).

Name resolution and typing. Check: overload resolution rules against MQL5 (which candidate wins for mixed numeric arguments, and whether an ambiguous call is an error rather than an arbitrary pick); implicit conversion rules and where a narrowing conversion is inserted silently; scoping and shadowing (an inner declaration that should shadow but resolves to the outer, or vice versa); forward references and declaration order; global vs local vs static storage; enum member resolution; struct member access and inheritance; the type of a comparison or arithmetic result; and whether an unresolved name is reported or silently bound to something plausible.

Lowering must preserve semantics exactly. Check: evaluation ORDER preserved when introducing temporaries (a temp that hoists a side-effecting call changes behaviour); compound assignment lowering evaluating the target expression twice (a[i++] += x); short-circuit operators lowered into non-short-circuit form; loop lowering preserving continue semantics (continue in a for loop must still run the increment - a while-based lowering that drops it creates an infinite loop); switch fallthrough and default placement; break targeting the correct construct in nested loops/switch; and the IR node set covering every construct the parser can produce (an unhandled node silently dropped is a P0).

scope: src/Modules/StrategyGovernance/YO4X.StrategyGovernance/Mql5BuiltinConstants.cs (~2048 lines), Mql5BuiltinSignatures.cs (~1250 lines), Mql5BuiltinCatalog.cs, Mql5BuiltinRealConstants.cs, Mql5PredefinedVariables.cs
focus: These tables must match the real MQL5 values exactly - a single wrong constant changes strategy behaviour with no error anywhere. Spot-check the highest-consequence values against the official MQL5 documentation: trade retcodes (10004/10006/10009/10013/10014/10015/10016/10019/10030), ENUM_ORDER_TYPE and ENUM_POSITION_TYPE ordinals, ENUM_TIMEFRAMES values (PERIOD_M1=1, PERIOD_H1=16385 etc - these are NOT sequential and are a classic error), ENUM_ORDER_TYPE_FILLING and TIME, ENUM_TRADE_REQUEST_ACTIONS, ENUM_SYMBOL_INFO_* and ENUM_ACCOUNT_INFO_* ordinals, error codes, MODE_* indicator constants, and colour constants. Also check signature arity and parameter types, by-ref parameters marked correctly, and default argument values. Report specific wrong values with the correct value.

Compiling untrusted source in isolation. Check: is the isolation boundary real (separate process, restricted account, working directory) or nominal; is there a hard TIMEOUT and is the process actually killed (and its children) when it expires; are temp/working directories unique per compile and cleaned on both success and failure; can a crafted source path or filename escape the working directory; are resource limits applied (memory, output size, disk); is compiler output captured with a size bound (unbounded capture of a compiler in a diagnostic loop exhausts memory); and is a failure surfaced accurately rather than reported as a successful compile of nothing.

This evidence is what justifies trusting a converted strategy. The key risk is a FALSE ATTESTATION: evidence that reports a clean conversion when something was dropped or changed. Check what the analyzer actually verifies versus what the evidence claims; whether an unsupported construct that was silently skipped is recorded; whether the evidence covers the whole source or only sampled parts; whether a failure to analyse produces evidence of success; and whether the formatter can be confused by attacker-controlled content in identifiers or comments (injection into the rendered report).

scope: src/Modules/StrategyGovernance/YO4X.StrategyGovernance/Mql5StaticInventory.cs, Mql5StaticInventoryAnalyzer.cs (~1068 lines), Mql5CompilePackageDossierPlanner.cs (~1147 lines), Mql5CompilePackagePlanFormatter.cs, Mql5InventoryFormatter.cs
focus: Inventory accuracy: does the analyzer detect every construct it claims to (a missed #include, a missed DLL import, a missed file or network call would let a dangerous strategy through); does it under-report on malformed input; is the plan deterministic for identical input (non-deterministic ordering from a hash set or dictionary iteration makes the dossier unreproducible, which defeats its purpose); and can attacker-controlled identifiers inject into the formatted output.

Pipeline wiring: are diagnostics from every stage actually collected and checked before proceeding (a stage whose errors are ignored lets broken code through), is the stage order correct, is state reset between compilations (leaked state between runs makes compile N depend on compile N-1 - a serious nondeterminism bug), and does the syntax model cover every construct the lexer/parser can produce.

The restricted subset is a security control: it defines what untrusted strategies may do. The critical question is ESCAPE - can a construct outside the subset reach compilation? Check whether the subset is enforced by an ALLOW-list (safe) or a DENY-list (fragile - anything not thought of is permitted); whether enforcement happens before or after any transformation that could reintroduce a forbidden construct; whether the check covers included files and macro-expanded code as well as the top-level source; and what happens on an unrecognised construct - it must be rejected, not passed through.

These verify that the converted strategy is equivalent to the original and that a runner is trusted. Ask what the equivalence check actually PROVES: comparing outputs over a sample of inputs is not equivalence, and if the sample is small or non-adversarial the attestation is close to meaningless - say so plainly. Check the tolerance used for floating comparison (too loose hides real divergence; too tight causes false alarms), what happens when the check is inconclusive (must not report equivalent), signature verification in the attestation verifier including constant-time comparison and issuer/expiry validation, and any path where verification is skipped.

Decoder: encoding detection and BOM handling, UTF-16 vs UTF-8 vs the ANSI codepage (real MQL5 files are often UTF-16LE), invalid byte sequences, and whether a decoding difference changes the code that gets compiled versus what a human reviewed. Secret scanner: FALSE NEGATIVES are the defect - what patterns does it miss (base64 blobs, keys split across lines, credentials in a comment or a string concatenation, non-ASCII), and does it scan the whole file including includes. MarkdownEscaper: does it escape every construct needed to prevent injection into a rendered report. CompilerOutputParser: parsing attacker-influenced compiler text - can crafted source produce output that the parser misreads as success.

Risk limits are the last line of defence before real money moves. Check: is every limit actually enforced on the order path or merely recorded; the comparison direction and boundary (greater-than vs greater-or-equal on a max exposure); what happens when a limit value is missing or null - it must fail CLOSED (block) rather than treat absent as unlimited; policy evaluation ORDER and whether a later permissive rule can override an earlier deny; aggregation across positions/accounts for portfolio-level limits; and whether the limit check and the order placement are atomic or a race can let two concurrent orders each pass a check they would jointly violate.

The permission model itself. Check: how a permission decision is reached and whether the default is deny; role/permission mapping and any wildcard or superuser shortcut; how the tenant is resolved for a request (from a validated token claim, or from a header/route value the caller controls - the latter is a P0 tenant-spoofing bypass); whether the resolved tenant is propagated to the data layer reliably and cannot be null; and whether identity comparison is case-sensitive/normalised consistently (a mismatch can grant or deny wrongly).

Approvals: can the requester also approve (missing separation of duties), can an approval be reused or replayed, is approval state checked at the moment of execution rather than only at request time. Audit: is the audit write in the same transaction as the audited action (otherwise actions occur unaudited), is the log append-only, are failures to audit ignored, and does it capture actor/target/before/after. Privacy: PII handling, redaction, deletion completeness. Support: any impersonation capability and whether it is audited and constrained.

Command contracts: versioning and whether an old message shape still deserialises correctly after a change (a silently-defaulted new field can mean a command executes with wrong parameters). Outbox module: the contract it exposes and whether it can guarantee what callers assume. Deployments: state machine and rollback. ReadModels: projection consistency, whether a projection can be rebuilt deterministically, and whether a failed projection update is retried or silently lost leaving the read model permanently stale.

SecretCoordination is the highest-value target: how secrets are distributed, who can request one, whether a request is authorised and audited, secret lifetime and revocation, and whether secret material can reach a log or an exception. GatewayGovernance: policy enforcement and fail-closed behaviour. BrokerAccounts: account ownership checks and credential linkage. RuntimeOperations: privileged operations and their authorisation.

Version identity: is a version derived from content (a hash) or a counter, and can two different sources produce the same identity (collision - the wrong strategy could then be deployed) or the same source produce two identities (breaking dedup and caching). Check comparison and ordering semantics, equality and GetHashCode consistency, and parsing/formatting round-trip.

Generator structure. The most valuable thing to find here is STATE LEAKAGE between runs: any static or instance field that is not reset per compilation, a cached name table, a counter, or a collection reused across generations - this makes compile N depend on compile N-1 and produces nondeterministic output for identical input. Also check pass ordering, whether diagnostics are collected and checked before emitting, and error handling that could emit a partial program.

Declaration emission. Check: MQL5 default initialisation (variables are zero-initialised; if the emitted C# leaves a field uninitialised or uses a different default, behaviour diverges); static local variables preserving value across calls and initialised once; global variable lifetime and initialisation ORDER (MQL5 initialises globals in declaration order - a different order changes behaviour); array declarations including fixed-size, dynamic, and multidimensional, and the distinction between MQL5 value-copy and C# reference semantics for arrays and structs (an assignment that aliases where MQL5 would copy is a P1 that corrupts data silently); struct field layout and defaults; enum underlying type; and input/extern parameters.

Statement emission. Check: for-loop with continue must still execute the increment (a lowering to while that drops it creates an infinite loop - P0); do-while condition evaluation; switch semantics - MQL5 allows fallthrough between cases whereas C# forbids implicit fallthrough, so check how this is bridged and whether a fallthrough case silently loses its fallthrough behaviour; break/continue targeting the correct enclosing construct when nested; return in a void function and missing return paths; declaration scoping inside blocks; and empty or single-statement bodies emitted without braces creating a dangling-else.

Call emission. Check: MQL5 by-reference parameters (&) mapped to C# ref/out correctly, and that an argument passed by reference is actually written back (a by-value emission silently discards the callee's writes - a very common and consequential bug, e.g. a function that fills an array or returns a value through a parameter); array parameters which are by-reference in MQL5; argument EVALUATION ORDER preserved when side effects are present; default argument values applied at the correct site; overload selection matching the binder's choice; and the argument order not being reversed or shifted for builtins.

Emitted-source correctness. Check: identifier mangling and collision - can two distinct MQL5 names map to the same C# identifier (silently merging two variables is a P0), and are C# reserved words escaped; string literal re-emission preserving escapes exactly (a quote or backslash mishandled changes the literal or breaks compilation); numeric literal formatting under a non-invariant culture (a comma decimal separator emits invalid C#); shadowed-local renaming preserving the correct binding at every use site; and generated code being valid C# for edge cases like empty bodies or deeply nested expressions.

Assembly identity and the codegen/runtime contract. Check: is the generated assembly name unique per strategy version (a reused name can collide in a load context or cause the wrong assembly to be resolved); is the contract between the emitted code and YO4X.Mql5.Runtime versioned, and would a runtime signature change be caught at build time or only fail at run time (a silent contract drift means emitted code calls a method whose meaning changed); deterministic output for identical input; and cleanup of emitted artefacts.

Array functions: ArrayResize semantics (MQL5 preserves existing elements and has a reserve parameter; it returns the new size or -1 on error), ArrayCopy with overlapping ranges and count/start semantics, ArrayInitialize, ArrayFill, ArraySort direction, ArrayBsearch, ArrayMaximum/ArrayMinimum returning an INDEX not a value, ArrayRange/ArraySize on multidimensional arrays, and above all AS-SERIES indexing: MQL5 series arrays are indexed with 0 = most recent bar, so any function that ignores the as-series flag reads the array backwards and every strategy using it trades on reversed data (P0). String functions: StringSubstr with out-of-range or negative arguments (MQL5 returns empty rather than throwing), StringFind return of -1, StringSplit, StringTrim, StringReplace return values, StringLen with non-ASCII, and 0-based vs 1-based position conventions.

CopyRates/CopyBuffer/CopyTime/CopyOpen/CopyHigh/CopyLow/CopyClose/CopyTickVolume: the start_pos and count semantics, the DIRECTION of the returned array (MQL5 returns data with index 0 as the oldest in the copied range unless the destination is set as-series - getting this backwards silently reverses every price series, P0), the return value being the number of elements copied or -1, and behaviour when fewer bars are available than requested. Also iBars/iTime/iClose style accessors and their shift semantics, Bars() counting, SymbolInfoDouble/Integer/String property mapping to the right values (point, digits, tick size, tick value, volume min/max/step, stops level, freeze level, contract size, swap, margin), and what is returned for an unknown symbol or property - a silent 0 for tick size or volume step causes a division by zero or an invalid lot size downstream.

Indicator handle lifecycle: iMA/iRSI/etc returning a handle, INVALID_HANDLE on failure, whether handles are cached and reused for identical parameters (unbounded handle creation in OnTick is a resource leak), IndicatorRelease, and CopyBuffer semantics including the buffer index, direction, and the return value. Terminal: TerminalInfoInteger/String property values, IsStopped/IsConnected, and any property returning a plausible but wrong default. Chart object store: unbounded growth of chart objects created per tick, and name collision handling.

scope: src/Runtime/YO4X.Mql5.Runtime/Mql5Runtime.cs, Mql5Runtime.Globals.cs, Mql5Runtime.Refused.cs, Mql5RuntimeOptions.cs, Mql5ZeroedInstance.cs, Mql5TypeInfo.cs, Mql5Structs.cs
focus: Mql5Runtime.Refused is a security control listing operations the runtime refuses - check its COMPLETENESS: is every dangerous MQL5 capability actually refused (FileOpen and the file family, WebRequest, SendMail, SendNotification, SendFTP, DLL imports, Sleep, ShellExecute-like calls, terminal control)? Anything reachable but not refused is an escape from the sandbox. Also check whether a refusal throws or returns a benign value (a silent benign return makes a strategy behave differently rather than failing loudly), global variable state shared across strategy instances (cross-strategy contamination), zero-initialisation correctness per type, and thread safety of any shared static state.

scope: src/Runtime/YO4X.Mql5.Runtime/Mql5Constants.cs, Mql5ErrorCodes.cs, Mql5Colors.cs, Mql5Log.cs, Mql5ProgramInfo.cs, Mql5UnsupportedOperationException.cs, IMql5MarketContext.cs, IMql5Strategy.cs
focus: Constant values must match MQL5 exactly. Spot-check against the official documentation: ENUM_TIMEFRAMES (PERIOD_M1=1, M5=5, M15=15, M30=30, H1=16385, H4=16388, D1=16408, W1=32769, MN1=49153 - the non-sequential values are a classic source of error), error codes (ERR_NO_ERROR=0, and the 4xxx runtime range), MODE_* and PRICE_* constants, INVALID_HANDLE, WHOLE_ARRAY, EMPTY_VALUE (which is DBL_MAX in MQL5 - using 0 or NaN instead changes every indicator emptiness check), CLR_NONE and colour packing order (MQL5 colour is BGR not RGB). Also check the logging surface for leaking sensitive values.

These wrap the MQL5 selection model, which is stateful and easy to get wrong. Check: the Select/SelectByIndex/SelectByTicket pattern - after a failed selection, do the property accessors return stale data from the previous selection (a strategy then reads the WRONG position's volume or price and closes the wrong trade - P0), or a clear invalid value? Does Select return false correctly when nothing matches? Is the selection state per-instance or shared/static (shared state across strategies is a P0)? Also check property mapping for each accessor (volume, price open/current, SL, TP, profit, swap, commission, magic, type, time), history selection requiring a prior HistorySelect over a time range, and index-based iteration remaining valid while positions change.

scope: src/Runtime/YO4X.Mql5.Engine/Trading/ - all files EXCEPT Mql5SimulatedBroker.cs (Mql5ClosedTrade.cs, Mql5Constants.cs, Mql5Enums.cs, Mql5OrderEvent.cs, Mql5PendingOrder.cs, Mql5Position.cs)
focus: Position and order state plus P&L arithmetic. Check the profit formula for both directions (a Sell position profits when price falls - a sign error inverts every short trade), contract size and tick value application, whether swap and commission are included in the reported profit and in the closed-trade record, partial-close volume and average-price arithmetic, position state transitions, enum ordinal parity with MQL5, and use of double for accumulated P&L where error compounds. Also check that Mql5Position mutations cannot leave the object internally inconsistent (volume zero but still open).

Shared indicator infrastructure - a defect here corrupts every indicator at once. RollingWindow: ring-buffer index arithmetic, behaviour before the window is full, the modulo/wrap logic, whether the oldest element is evicted correctly, and off-by-one in the count. MovingAverageCalculator: all four MQL5 modes (SMA, EMA, SMMA/Wilder, LWMA) - EMA alpha must be 2/(n+1), SMMA must be 1/n, LWMA weights must be 1..n with the correct total; also the seeding of the first value and incremental-update drift versus a full recompute. Factory: correct dispatch from an MQL5 MA method/applied-price constant to the implementation, and behaviour on an unknown constant. Base: buffer indexing direction and warm-up handling.

Feed integrity determines whether a backtest means anything. CSV feed: parsing with CultureInfo.InvariantCulture (a comma-decimal locale silently misparses every price - P0), delimiter and header handling, malformed rows silently skipped versus failing, whether bars are validated as monotonically increasing in time, duplicate timestamps, gaps and weekends, and the OHLC invariant (High must be >= Open/Close and Low <= Open/Close - unvalidated bad data produces impossible fills). Also check unbounded loading of a large file into memory. DeterministicRandom: is it genuinely deterministic and seeded, does it produce the same sequence across runs and platforms. Synthetic feed: reproducibility and whether it can generate invalid bars.

scope:
src/Runtime/YO4X.Mql5.Engine/Hosting/** (IMql5Strategy.cs, Mql5RunOptions.cs, Mql5RunReport.cs, Mql5StrategyHost.cs)
src/Runtime/YO4X.Mql5.Engine/Context/** (IMql5MarketContext.cs, Mql5MarketContext.cs)
focus: The tick loop and lifecycle. Check: OnInit/OnTick/OnDeinit ordering and that a failed OnInit prevents trading; whether OnTick sees the bar being formed or only closed bars, and whether the context exposes the CURRENT bar's close before it is complete (look-ahead bias - P0); the order of feed advance, indicator update, broker update, and strategy callback within one step (updating the broker after the strategy decides, or indicators after the strategy reads them, produces off-by-one-bar behaviour); exception handling inside the loop (a swallowed strategy exception silently produces a no-trade run reported as success); run report accounting - trade count, win rate, drawdown and profit computed from the same source of truth as the broker; and state reset between runs.

The adapter between the platform and the real MT5 API - defects here move real money. Check: order request field mapping in both directions and any field dropped in translation (a dropped stop-loss on a live order is a P0); volume and price normalisation to the symbol's step and digits before sending; error/retcode translation and whether a rejection is distinguished from a success; timeout handling and what is assumed when a response never arrives (retrying an order whose outcome is unknown can duplicate it); connection loss and reconnect behaviour mid-order; and whether any operation is retried that is not idempotent.

This IPC channel carries broker commands and credentials, so it is a trust boundary. Check: how the peer is AUTHENTICATED and whether the check happens before any message is processed; whether the secret comparison is constant-time; the transport (named pipe ACLs, TCP binding to localhost only or to all interfaces - binding broadly would expose the trading control channel on the network, a P0); protocol framing - is a length prefix bounded (an unbounded length allows memory exhaustion), is a partial read handled, can a malformed frame desynchronise the stream; DESERIALIZATION of untrusted input (any polymorphic or type-name-based deserialisation is a remote code execution risk); and replay protection on command messages.

scope: src/Runtime/YO4X.Trading.ProcessIsolation/BrokerWorkerContractValidator.cs, BrokerWorkerContracts.cs, BrokerWorkerDeploymentPathPolicy.cs, BrokerWorkerLaunchManifest.cs, IsolatedBrokerConnectionProbeClient.cs, IsolatedBrokerProcessOptions.cs, IsolatedMt5ProcessGateway.cs
focus: Process launch is a classic injection point. Check: how the executable path is resolved and whether the path policy can be escaped (relative segments, symlinks, a writable directory allowing an attacker to plant a binary that then runs with the worker's privileges - P0); how arguments are constructed and whether any value (account id, symbol, path) is interpolated into a command line without quoting/escaping; whether credentials are passed on the command line (visible to other processes) or via environment/stdin; working directory and environment inheritance; process lifetime - is the child killed on parent exit and are orphans cleaned up; and manifest validation before launch.

Contract shape: nullability annotations on public members and whether a null can flow where the consumer assumes non-null; enum completeness against the MT5 domain and whether a default(enum) value is a valid meaningful member (a default that means Buy is dangerous); money and volume represented with an adequate type; any mutable shared type used as a message; and whether the interfaces force callers to check a result or make it easy to ignore a failure.

Serialization compatibility across process boundaries and versions. Check: whether adding or removing a field breaks older peers, whether an unknown field is rejected or ignored, default values for missing fields (a defaulted lot size or a defaulted enum silently changes a command's meaning), enum serialisation by name versus ordinal (ordinal is fragile to reordering), any polymorphic/type-name deserialisation, numeric precision preserved through the format, and whether the contract is versioned at all.

Gateway routing and protection: authentication and authorisation on every forwarded route, whether the target is chosen from caller-controlled input (an SSRF/open-proxy risk), header forwarding including any auth header passed to an unintended destination, backpressure and concurrency limits (an unbounded queue or unlimited concurrent connections is a DoS), timeouts on upstream calls, and error handling that could leak upstream detail to the caller.

Crash and restart behaviour of live strategies. Check: restart backoff - an immediate unbounded restart loop on a persistently failing strategy is a resource and broker-spam problem; restart LIMITS and whether a permanently broken strategy is eventually parked rather than restarted forever; and most importantly STATE AFTER RESTART - does the strategy resume with knowledge of its open positions, or can it re-enter a trade it already has (double exposure, P0)? Also check whether a supervisor crash leaves orphaned child processes, whether shutdown is graceful (positions handled per policy) and whether health reflects the strategy's real state rather than just process liveness.

The probe handles real broker credentials to test a connection. Check: whether credentials are logged, written to a temp file, included in an error message or exception, or left in memory longer than needed; timeout on the probe (a hung probe holding credentials); whether a probe failure is distinguished from a wrong-credentials result and whether repeated probing could trigger a broker-side lockout; and whether the probe can be invoked by an unauthorised caller.

Worker host lifecycle and the isolation boundary it is supposed to maintain: startup validation, what it accepts from the parent process and whether it trusts it, shutdown and cleanup of the MT5 terminal/connection, exception handling that keeps the host alive in a broken state, and whether it enforces any restriction on what the hosted code may do.

Windows DPAPI credential storage for broker credentials. Check: the protection SCOPE - CurrentUser versus LocalMachine (LocalMachine means any local user or process can decrypt, a serious weakening); whether optional entropy is used and where that entropy is stored (entropy stored next to the ciphertext adds nothing); file location and ACLs on the vault file and its directory; whether plaintext is written to a temp file or left in a string that is never cleared (SecureString or explicit clearing versus a normal string that lingers in the heap and could reach a crash dump); error handling that could log the plaintext; atomic write and corruption handling; and whether deletion actually removes the material.

scope: mt5-net-api-full-binaries-main/** (also check .gitattributes for LFS handling and any reference to these binaries from csproj files)
focus: Supply chain. Establish what this directory actually is: which DLLs/executables are present, their apparent origin and version, and whether any checksum, signature, or provenance record exists in the repo. Then assess: is the version PINNED and verifiable, or could it be silently swapped; is it referenced directly by project files (find the references); is a binary committed that could instead come from a package feed; is there a licence file; and what capability does it expose to the platform (network, filesystem, native interop). Report what you can establish from the repository contents - do not speculate about the contents of binaries you cannot read, and say plainly what could not be determined.

Command-line argument parsing and validation (missing, malformed, or out-of-range values silently defaulted), determinism of a run given identical inputs, exit codes reflecting success or failure (a tool that exits 0 on failure breaks any automation depending on it), output format stability, and unbounded memory use on a large backtest.

These tools handle credentials directly. Check: are secrets accepted as command-line ARGUMENTS (visible in the process list and shell history - a real defect; stdin or a file with restricted permissions is correct); are they echoed to the console or a log; is an input file deleted or left behind; what permissions are set on anything written; and does DevelopmentBootstrap create any account, key, or credential with a default/weak value that could survive into a non-development environment.

Market data integrity - corrupt history silently invalidates every backtest run against it. Check: duplicate bar detection and how a duplicate timestamp is resolved; gap detection and whether gaps are filled with synthetic data (which would be a serious silent fabrication) or left as gaps; timezone handling on imported timestamps and whether the broker offset is recorded; OHLC validation; numeric parsing with invariant culture; partial-import failure leaving an incomplete dataset that looks complete; and idempotency of a re-run.

The highest-value question: can any of these tools, which are intended for DEMO accounts, act against a LIVE account? Check how demo versus live is determined and whether that check is enforced before any order is placed (a tool that executes a test trade on a live account is a P0). Also check credential handling, whether account details are printed or logged, and whether the canary/execution test cleans up the positions it opens.

EndpointDiscovery: is a discovered endpoint trusted and used without validation (connecting to an attacker-supplied broker endpoint would expose credentials), and is TLS verified. SymbolImport: symbol property mapping precision (tick size, volume step, contract size - a wrong value silently produces invalid orders) and handling of an unknown or renamed symbol. LiveBots: anything here touching a live account needs an explicit guard - check what prevents accidental live execution and whether credentials or account ids are hardcoded.

scope: whole tree - CROSS-CUTTING sweep. File findings ONLY about logging and information disclosure.
focus: Sweep for sensitive data reaching a log, a console, an exception message, or an HTTP response. Look for: broker passwords, investor passwords, API keys, tokens, connection strings, and DPAPI/key material written via any logger, Console.Write, or string interpolation into an exception; whole request/response bodies or headers logged (Authorization headers in particular); account numbers, login ids, balances and positions logged at a level that reaches shared infrastructure; exception detail, stack traces, or SQL text returned to an HTTP client; PII in audit or diagnostic output without redaction; and log statements inside a tight loop or per-tick path that would flood storage. Also check whether any structured-logging destructuring would serialise an entire credential-bearing object. Report the worst instances with file:line, and say for each what exactly would be exposed and to whom.

scope: whole tree - CROSS-CUTTING sweep. File findings ONLY about exception handling.
focus: Sweep for swallowed and mishandled exceptions. Look for: empty catch blocks; catch blocks that only log and then continue as if the operation succeeded; catch (Exception) around a money path (order placement, balance update, position close) where the caller cannot distinguish failure from success; a caught exception that returns a default/success-shaped value (returning false, null, or an empty collection where the caller treats it as a legitimate empty result); catch blocks that lose the original exception (throw ex resetting the stack trace); exceptions swallowed inside a background loop so the loop dies or silently stops making progress; and finally/using blocks that can themselves throw and mask the original error. Prioritise the trading, worker, and persistence paths - a swallowed exception there means an order or a state change silently did not happen. Report the worst instances with file:line and state what silently fails.

scope: whole tree - CROSS-CUTTING sweep. File findings ONLY about async/await correctness.
focus: Sweep for: .Result, .Wait(), .GetAwaiter().GetResult() blocking on async code (deadlock risk and thread-pool starvation); async void methods outside event handlers (an exception there crashes the process and cannot be awaited); missing CancellationToken parameters or a token accepted and then not passed through to the inner call (making shutdown and timeouts ineffective); fire-and-forget tasks with no exception observation; ConfigureAwait usage in library code; Task.Run wrapping already-async work; async lambdas passed where an Action is expected (silently becoming async void); a lock held across an await; and unawaited Task returns. Prioritise the API hosts, workers, and the trading path where a deadlock stalls order processing. Report the worst instances with file:line and the concrete consequence.

scope: whole tree - CROSS-CUTTING sweep. File findings ONLY about resource lifetime and disposal.
focus: Sweep for undisposed or mis-disposed resources: NpgsqlConnection/Command/DataReader and transactions created without using or disposed only on the success path (a leaked connection under load exhausts the pool and takes the whole service down); FileStream and other streams; HttpClient created per request (socket exhaustion) or a static HttpClient without connection lifetime management; Process objects not disposed and child processes not killed; Timer instances never disposed (they keep firing after their owner is gone); CancellationTokenSource not disposed; SemaphoreSlim and other synchronisation primitives; IDisposable fields on a class that does not itself implement IDisposable; and a using scope that ends before an async operation using the resource completes. Report the worst instances with file:line and the failure mode under sustained load.

scope: whole tree - CROSS-CUTTING sweep. File findings ONLY about injection.
focus: Sweep for injection of every kind: SQL built by string concatenation or interpolation where any part comes from user input or from data previously stored from user input (second-order injection) - check every Npgsql command construction, and note that a table or column name cannot be parameterised so any dynamic identifier is a risk that needs an allow-list; command/process injection where a value is interpolated into a command line or a shell invocation; PATH TRAVERSAL where a filename, strategy name, corpus id, or archive entry name is joined into a path without canonicalisation and containment checking (this codebase handles uploaded MQL5 files and archives, so check that specifically); unsafe deserialization including any type-name-driven or polymorphic deserialisation of untrusted input; LDAP/XML/regex injection; and regex built from user input or a catastrophically backtracking pattern applied to user input. Report with file:line and a concrete exploit path.

scope: all appsettings*.json, Properties/launchSettings.json, compose.yaml, .env.example, global.json, Directory.Build.props, *.pubxml - CROSS-CUTTING sweep. File findings ONLY about configuration.
focus: Sweep configuration for insecure defaults and environment bleed. Check: any credential, key, or connection string with a real-looking value committed; development settings that would apply in production (detailed errors, Swagger, permissive CORS, disabled HTTPS redirection, a development authentication scheme); a required setting with an insecure fallback when absent; logging levels that would emit sensitive data; compose.yaml exposing a database or internal service port publicly, using default credentials, or running without TLS; a database connection with SSL Mode=Disable or Prefer; and settings that differ between hosts in a way that suggests one was forgotten. For each, say which environment is affected and what the consequence is.

scope: all *.csproj, Directory.Packages.props, Directory.Build.props, global.json, src/Frontend/YO4X.Web/package.json - CROSS-CUTTING sweep. File findings ONLY about build and dependencies.
focus: Sweep the build. Check: central package management consistency and any package version overridden locally; floating version ranges (* or a wildcard) that make builds non-reproducible; packages with known-vulnerable versions - name the package and version and say what the advisory is, but only where you are confident, and mark uncertain ones as PLAUSIBLE; TargetFramework consistency across projects and any project on an older framework; whether nullable reference types and warnings-as-errors are enabled consistently (a project with nullable disabled silently loses null safety); analyzers enabled; whether a test project is referenced by a production project; and whether any project references the development identity project. Also check the npm dependency set for the same issues.

scope: scripts/*.ps1, scripts/*.mjs, scripts/*.sql, src/Frontend/YO4X.Web/scripts/*.mjs - CROSS-CUTTING sweep. File findings ONLY about the scripts.
focus: Sweep the operational scripts. Check: credentials or connection strings hardcoded or echoed to the console; a secret passed as a command-line argument; Invoke-Expression or equivalent applied to a value that could come from input; a path built from a variable without quoting; destructive operations (Remove-Item -Recurse -Force, DROP, TRUNCATE, git reset --hard, database drops) without a confirmation, a target check, or an environment guard - a script that can drop a production database because an environment variable was unset is a P0; missing error handling so a failed step is silently skipped and the script reports success; and whether $ErrorActionPreference is set so failures actually stop the script.

scope: workers, stores, hosts, and any shared state across the tree - CROSS-CUTTING sweep. File findings ONLY about concurrency.
focus: Sweep for concurrency defects: non-atomic check-then-act (read a row or a flag, decide, then write - two callers both pass the check, which on an order path means two orders); lost updates from read-modify-write without optimistic concurrency or a lock; static or singleton mutable state accessed from multiple requests or threads (Dictionary and List are not thread-safe - concurrent writes can corrupt them or loop forever); a scoped service captured by a singleton; lock ordering that could deadlock; a lock held across an await or across an I/O call; double-checked locking done incorrectly; missing volatile or Interlocked on a flag polled by another thread; and collection modified while being enumerated. Prioritise the order path, the work queue, and any cache. Report with file:line and the interleaving that breaks it.

scope: whole tree - CROSS-CUTTING sweep. File findings ONLY about date and time handling.
focus: Sweep for time defects, which matter unusually much in trading. Look for: DateTime.Now where DateTime.UtcNow is required (any timestamp compared across machines or persisted); DateTime with Kind Unspecified persisted or compared; a timestamp read from Postgres as timestamp rather than timestamptz losing the offset; mixing BROKER SERVER time with UTC or local time (MQL5 TimeCurrent is server time - comparing it to a UtcNow-derived value is wrong by the broker offset, silently shifting every session filter and time-based rule); DST transition handling and whether a broker offset is treated as fixed; day-of-week conventions and off-by-one (MQL5 MqlDateTime uses Sunday=0); date arithmetic using AddDays across a DST boundary; a timeout or interval computed by subtracting two differently-kinded times; and formatting/parsing without an invariant culture. Report with file:line and the concrete shift it causes.

scope: the command, outbox, broker, and API mutation paths - CROSS-CUTTING sweep. File findings ONLY about idempotency and duplicate execution.
focus: Sweep for places where a retry can cause a duplicate effect. Trace the path from an API mutation through the command handler, the outbox, and the broker adapter, and at each hop ask: if this step runs twice, what happens? Look for: mutation endpoints with no idempotency key, or a key accepted but never enforced by a unique constraint; a retry policy wrapping a non-idempotent operation; an operation whose effect is applied before its completion is recorded (a crash between them re-runs the effect); a message acknowledged before its effect is durable, or a durable effect with no acknowledgement (re-delivery); and any place a timeout is treated as a definite failure and retried when the outcome is actually unknown. On this platform a duplicate means a duplicate ORDER, so treat a confirmed duplicate path as P0. Report with file:line and the exact sequence that duplicates.

scope: whole tree - CROSS-CUTTING sweep. File findings ONLY about nullability.
focus: Sweep for nullability defects that hide real NullReferenceExceptions. Look for: the null-forgiving operator (!) applied to a value that genuinely can be null, especially on data read from the database or deserialised from a request; public contract members annotated non-nullable but assigned from a nullable source without a check; #nullable disable in a file or a project with nullable turned off entirely (silently losing all null safety there); a nullable value dereferenced after a check that does not actually narrow it; and a nullable database column read into a non-nullable property. Prioritise public contracts, deserialisation boundaries, and data-access code. Report with file:line and the input that produces the NRE.

scope: whole tree - CROSS-CUTTING sweep. File findings ONLY about unbounded resource use.
focus: Sweep for missing limits. Look for: a database query with no LIMIT or paging that grows with tenant data (loading every journal row or every equity-curve point into memory); ToList/ToArray materialising an unbounded result; a request body, uploaded file, or archive read fully into memory with no size cap (this platform accepts uploaded MQL5 sources and archives - check that specifically, including decompression bombs); a collection, cache, or dictionary that only ever grows (chart objects, indicator handles, connection entries) with no eviction; string concatenation in a loop over unbounded input; unbounded recursion on attacker-influenced input such as a deeply nested expression in the MQL5 parser (stack overflow crashes the process); unbounded concurrency (an unlimited number of parallel tasks or connections); and a log written per tick. Report with file:line and the input size that causes failure.

Judge whether these tests would actually CATCH a regression. For each significant test area ask: does it assert a real invariant, or only that a call did not throw? Look specifically for: tests that assert a row was written but never that its VALUES are correct; tenant-isolation tests that only test the happy path and never assert that another tenant's data is inaccessible; concurrency and queue-claim tests that run sequentially and therefore prove nothing about the concurrent behaviour they are named for; tests that would still pass if the tenant predicate were removed from the query; assertions on a count rather than on content; and shared mutable fixture state that makes tests order-dependent. Name the specific behaviour that is claimed to be covered but is not, and the bug that would slip through.

The central question for these tests: what is the ORACLE? An indicator or runtime test is only meaningful if the expected values come from a trustworthy reference (real MetaTrader output, or an independently derived value). If the expected values were generated by running this same implementation, the test locks in whatever bug exists and proves nothing - identify any test where that appears to be the case and say so, because it is the most valuable finding here. Also check: tolerance on floating comparisons (too loose to detect a real formula error); whether warm-up and seeding behaviour is tested; whether the as-series/index-direction convention is tested; whether edge cases (division by zero, insufficient bars, flat price) are covered; and which indicators or runtime functions have no test at all.

Money-path coverage. Determine whether the following are actually tested and asserted, and name any that are not: duplicate order submission under retry; a broker response that times out with an unknown outcome; risk limits at their exact boundary; an order rejected by the broker and the resulting local state; partial fills; reconciliation of local state against broker state; and illegal state transitions being rejected. Also check for over-mocking - if the coordinator's collaborators are all mocked, the test may assert only that a mock was called and would pass even if the real integration were broken. Name the specific untested branch and the bug it hides.

Architecture tests first: read what rules they actually enforce and check whether the rules are real constraints or trivially satisfied - a dependency rule that lists no violations because its filter matches nothing is worse than no test, so verify each rule actually selects the types it claims to. Boundary tests: is every endpoint covered for the UNAUTHORISED and WRONG-TENANT cases, not just the authorised happy path (an authz test suite that only tests success proves nothing about the guard); is middleware order tested; are error responses asserted not to leak detail. Name specific gaps.
